title: The Inputs-Outputs Question
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart introduces a framing question from colleague Laura Gersch — plotting teacher effort (inputs) against student learning (outputs) — as the organizing lens for a new blog series. He walks through a progression of four quadrants: low-input/low-output work that's indefensible, high-input/low-output work that causes burnout, high-input/high-output work that many teachers wrongly treat as the aspirational ceiling, and finally the 'sweet spot' of high output achieved with lower input, reached by identifying and cutting practices that don't actually move student learning. He explicitly disclaims perfectionism, saying he isn't chasing a mythical maximum-output-zero-input ideal but a realistic 'Target Zone.' The piece closes by announcing that the upcoming series will apply this inputs-outputs lens to student motivation via his five key beliefs framework, arguing that instructional practices conducive to cultivating those beliefs have given him more return on effort than anything else in his career.
points: Stuart's inputs-outputs grid reframes 'what's the work that matters most' as a geometry problem: plotting teacher effort against student learning to locate practices in a genuine low-input/high-output sweet spot.

He names and rejects the common assumption that maxed-out effort and maxed-out results is the aspirational ceiling for teaching, arguing many teachers wrongly treat sustained overwork as the only path to excellence.

The pivotal move in his framework is discovering that some high-effort practices contribute little to actual student learning — meaning the path to the sweet spot runs through subtraction (skipping or satisficing), not just addition.
He explicitly disclaims perfectionism, aiming for a realistic 'Target Zone' rather than the theoretical maximum-output/zero-input ideal, which he says would take superhuman effort to reach.
quotes: What's the work within the Inputs-Outputs sweet spot? If you put inputs on the y-axis and outputs on the x, Laura asked — what's in the sweet spot of low input and high output?
Tons of effort in (inputs), only to arrive at the end of the lesson or unit or semester and realize, "Dang! The students didn't learn!" This is the kind of stuff that burns us out.

There are plenty of others who believe that this is the only way to get maxed-out results, and that since they don't have that kind of time or energy or skill, they're not ever going to get great results in their classroom. But what if there were ways to produce more learning with less stress?
It turns out that some of the stuff I spend lots of effort on (stuff that I input) isn't actually doing much for student learning (the thing I'm trying to output).
I'm not a perfectionist kind of guy any more, so I'm not really aiming in my practice or my research or my writing for that mythical Circle 5 in the preceding graphic.

I can't think of anything in my career that has given me more bang for my buck — in the language of today's blog post, more output for my input — than becoming strong at instructional practices that are highly conducive to 5KB cultivation.
